title: A case of Lymphoplasmacyte-rich meningioma mimicking pachymeningitis
case_prompt:
A 55-year-old woman was evaluated for a 4-year history of episodic psychiatric symptoms, headache, and seizures. In June 2016, she developed irritability, auditory hallucinations, and delusions; a brain CT showed left frontal dural hyperdensity. Her symptoms improved with risperidone. In November 2016, she had acute severe headache, drowsiness, dullness, and seizures; MRI with contrast showed linear dural enhancement over the left frontal convexity and falx cerebri. Pachymeningitis was favored, and differential diagnoses included meningioma, lymphoma, neurosarcoidosis, Rosai-Dorfman disease, and Erdheim-Chester disease, but the patient refused a dural biopsy. Over the next 4 years, her episodic symptoms remitted with intermittent mannitol and diazepam; annual MRIs showed no change until December 2019, when CT and contrast MRI revealed a growing left frontal dural mass with more diffuse enhancement. 
In April 2020, on admission, she was alert and oriented but slightly apathetic; cognitive function was intact and a right Chaddock sign was present. Laboratory tests were unremarkable except for an elevated serum IgG level of 18.1 g/L (reference range 7.51–15.6 g/L). Lumbar puncture showed an opening pressure of 200 mm H₂O; cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed normal cell count, glucose, protein, and chloride, undetectable CSF IgG4, and no malignant cells.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Idiopathic hypertrophic pachymeningitis was initially favored because of linear dural enhancement without mass, but “long-term stability without corticotherapy is rare in this disease… episodic symptoms could resolve spontaneously which made the diagnosis of IPH doubtable.”
2. En plaque meningioma was considered because of carpet-like dural involvement, but “they are more inclined to involve sphenoid wing rather than convexity. Dramatic osseous destruction is also an important feature.”
3. Primary pachymeningeal lymphoma was included, but “Leptomeningeal involvement and parenchymal infiltration are common in pachymeningeal lymphoma,” which were absent here.
4. IgG4-related pachymeningitis was considered among non-neoplastic causes, but “IgG4-related pachymeningitis… was not supported by ancillary testing or pathology.”
5. Neurosarcoidosis was in the differential, but “neurosarcoidosis… was not supported by ancillary testing or pathology.”
6. Rosai-Dorfman disease was included, but “Rosai Dorfman disease… was not supported by ancillary testing or pathology.”
7. Erdheim-Chester disease was considered, but “Erdheim Chester disease was not supported by ancillary testing or pathology.”
